basic_info.basic_info: Course sequencing & finale is the deliberate ordering of a multi-stop date so that the single most intense, positive, memorable moment lands at or near the END, with a strong 'peak' somewhere in the middle, because retrospective memory of the whole date is dominated by its peak and its ending rather than its average or duration. It leverages Kahneman's peak-end rule and duration neglect. Unlike 'activity variety/pacing' (which manages moment-to-moment engagement) or 'atmosphere/mood' (which shapes the ambient feeling), this factor is specifically about the MEMORY the date leaves once it is over, i.e. the impression that drives whether there's a next date. Its distinct mechanism: engineer the remembered self's summary, not just the experiencing self's minute-by-minute pleasure.

rationale.psychology: Core evidence: (1) Peak-end rule (Kahneman, Fredrickson, Redelmeier and colleagues): people judge past experiences almost entirely by the average of the most intense moment (peak) and the final moment (end), not the sum or average of the whole. Redelmeier & Kahneman (1996) studied colonoscopy/lithotripsy patients and found remembered discomfort tracked peak and end pain, not the experience's total; a follow-up (Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber & Redelmeier, 1993, 'When more pain is preferred to less') showed adding extra but milder discomfort at the end IMPROVED the overall memory, proving endings are weighted heavily. (2) Duration neglect (Redelmeier & Kahneman, 1996): the correlation between how long the procedure lasted and its remembered unpleasantness was near zero (~.03) - length barely matters to memory, so a shorter date with a great ending beats a long one that fizzles. (3) Experiencing self vs. remembering self (Kahneman, 2011, 'Thinking, Fast and Slow'): the remembering self decides whether to repeat an experience, and it is governed by peak-end + duration neglect; since a second date is a decision of the remembering self, the ending is disproportionately decisive. (4) Serial-position / recency effect (Murdock, 1962): the last items in a sequence are recalled best, reinforcing that the final segment is over-represented in memory. (5) Positive-experience version: Do, Rupert & Wolford (2008, 'Evaluations of Pleasurable Experiences: The Peak-End Rule') extended the effect to pleasant experiences, and boundary-condition work (e.g. Wharton studies on multi-episode events) shows the rule holds when episodes form a coherent 'gestalt,' as a date does. Together these imply: place the emotional high point late, finish on a clearly positive, upbeat note, and don't dilute the ending by dragging the date on past its peak.

application.how_to_apply: Concrete actions: (1) Design the course as a rising arc: open with a low-stakes warm-up (coffee/walk), build to a genuine PEAK (a shared thrill, a great meal, a beautiful view, a fun activity), and reserve a strong, positive moment for the very END. (2) Make the finale emotionally intense and pleasant, not merely convenient: a night view, dessert at a special spot, a sunset, live music, a small surprise, or simply the most connected conversation - something that will be the last thing remembered. (3) END ON A HIGH, don't let the date decay: leave while things are still good rather than stretching until you're both tired, bored, or awkward; a crisp, upbeat goodbye beats a long fizzle. (4) Exploit duration neglect: prefer a shorter, well-shaped date over a marathon; more hours do not buy a better memory, a better peak and ending do. (5) Put any dull-but-necessary logistics (queues, transit, parking) in the MIDDLE, never at the finish. (6) Sequence multiple venues so intensity generally climbs (e.g. casual -> lively -> intimate/scenic) rather than front-loading the best part first. (7) Create a clean 'end marker': a memorable last line, a small shared ritual, or a warm parting gesture, so the ending is vivid and positive. (8) For an established relationship, still cap experiences on a high note (leave the party/trip segment while it's fun) to bank a better memory.

common_mistakes.common_mistakes: Front-loading the best activity first so the date declines and the last impression is flat; ending on a logistical low - a stressful drive, a long line, a rushed check-split, or a tired, aimless 'what now?' stretch; over-extending the date past its natural peak so fatigue and awkwardness become the final memory (violating end-on-a-high); assuming a LONGER date equals a better date (duration neglect says otherwise); making the finale merely 'convenient' (nearest station) instead of emotionally strong; manufacturing a forced, over-the-top 'grand finale' that feels inauthentic or pressuring, especially early on; and neglecting the peak entirely so the date is pleasant-but-forgettable with no high point for memory to latch onto.

examples.examples: (1) First date arc: coffee and a stroll (warm-up) -> a fun interactive activity like a pottery class or arcade (peak) -> dessert at a rooftop with a night view as the finale, then a warm goodbye while energy is still high - the last, most-remembered beat is the view + connection. (2) Duration-neglect design: instead of a 6-hour marathon that peters out, a tight 2.5-hour date that ends right after the best moment, banking a stronger memory. (3) Sequencing fix: a couple planning dinner + a concert deliberately puts DINNER first and the CONCERT last so the emotional high (live music) is the ending, rather than eating after the show and finishing on a quiet, deflated note. (4) End marker: closing the evening at a small gelato spot with a shared last-bite ritual and a memorable parting line, so the date is remembered as sweet and upbeat.
